title: Empowering Educators in AI: Insights from Co-Designing an AI Microcredential with and for K-12 Educators
extended_summary:
This paper asks what professional learning needs K-12 educators anticipate when integrating AI into their classrooms, and how those needs can inform the design of an AI professional development microcredential. Rather than evaluating an instructional intervention with outcome measures, the study focuses on a co-design process that surfaces educator priorities, concerns, and desired features for AI-focused professional learning.

The authors worked with six participants: four middle school teachers and two instructional coaches/facilitators. Across three one-hour co-design sessions, participants completed semi-structured focus groups and a card-sorting activity to rank professional learning statements (e.g., what they can, want to, will, and need to do). The project produced an initial conjecture map for an Introduction to AI microcredential and iterative revisions based on educator feedback. The microcredential was intended for global use by teachers with varying AI experience and was not tied to a specific AI product.

The main findings emphasize that teachers want AI PD that is ethical, practical, unbiased, standards-aligned, and quick to use. Key themes included the need to teach ethical AI integration, the reality that teacher agency is constrained by district and standards requirements, the desire for unfiltered and critical understanding of AI limitations, the importance of modernizing classrooms on teachers’ own terms, and the need for continuous just-in-time learning rather than one-off sessions. The paper also describes example microcredential activities, including bias exploration with Teachable Machine and scenario-based ethics reflection tasks, as design responses to these themes.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative co-design study using focus groups, card sorting, inductive coding, and conjecture mapping. It provides useful design evidence, but it does not test intervention efficacy or include a comparison group.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper has clear relevance for AI professional development design in K-12 settings, but it reports no measurable outcome effect sizes or direct impact on student or teacher performance. Its impact is therefore promising but still indirect and mainly formative.

interventions.use_case: Co-design and development of an AI microcredential for K-12 educators, including short asynchronous modules, AI ethics scenarios, bias exploration with Teachable Machine, and reflection activities to support classroom AI integration.

finding.finding_summary: This is a qualitative co-design/design-research paper focused on building a teacher AI microcredential, not a causal impact study. The paper reports that educator input materially reshaped the course design toward short, actionable, standards-aligned, ethics-focused professional learning resources that can be used across school contexts (n=6 co-design participants, plus anecdotal feedback from n=8 elementary educators on one activity).
finding.measure: Co-design session themes, conjecture map revisions, and qualitative feedback from focus groups/card sorting
finding.study_size: n=6 co-design participants; anecdotal feedback from n=8 elementary educators

finding.finding_summary: Educators repeatedly requested quick, easily accessible, asynchronous learning activities and just-in-time resources that would not add to workload. The resulting microcredential was redesigned to include short videos (less than 5 minutes) and short activities estimated to take less than 15 minutes, indicating a practical efficiency-oriented design response rather than measured productivity gains.
finding.measure: Educator preferences for PD format; design requirements translated into module length and activity duration

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes teacher development of AI literacy, critical evaluation of tools, and reflective judgment about ethical and classroom use of AI. It also reports that teachers wanted resources to help them modernize instruction on their own terms and make informed decisions about AI tool selection and standards alignment, but these are qualitative design findings rather than measured learning gains.
finding.measure: Qualitative themes about AI literacy, agency, and reflective practice
